teaser.text: NVIDIA is a company that sells the machinery and software for demanding computing. Its business is easiest to understand as a flow: customers pay for a connected platform, NVIDIA pays the specialists and employees who build it, and the difference becomes profit.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for NVIDIA Corporation, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The bear case starts at $400,000 million of revenue. Growth then falls to 30%, 5% and negative 10%, with margins declining from 48% to 45% and then 42%. The bull case starts at $430,000 million, grows by 80%, 45% and 30%, and holds margins near recent levels at 56% and then 57%. These differences reflect NVIDIA’s history of growth slowing from 114.2% to 65.5%, alongside the risk that customer payback, custom chips or supply constraints weaken demand. The latest quarter delivered $96,221 million of revenue and $59,688 million of net income. The forecast excludes $23,707 million of equity-security gains and a $711 million tax release because they are not operating earnings.

blocks.heading: How much cash does NVIDIA Corporation really make?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow subtracts capital spending from cash generated by operations. “Real free cash flow” subtracts stock pay as well, treating employee equity awards as an economic cost to shareholders. The difference matters because stock compensation transfers value to employees through additional shares.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay today for NVIDIA Corporation's earnings and cash?

paragraphs.text: Price-to-earnings, or P/E, compares the share price with profit per share. It tells investors how many dollars they pay for one dollar of annual earnings. A forward P/E uses expected earnings rather than earnings already earned. If a share costs $100 and current earnings are $10, the P/E is 10 times. If expected earnings rise to $20, the forward P/E falls to 5 times without the share price changing. The lower multiple is therefore partly a bet that the forecast will arrive.

Gross margin is the share of sales left after the direct cost of making and delivering products. If it falls from 75% to 70%, NVIDIA keeps less from every dollar of revenue before paying for research, staff, taxes, and other costs. Free cash flow is the cash left after running the business and making necessary investments. It is closer to the money available for repurchases, dividends, or debt reduction.

blocks.heading: Is NVIDIA Corporation’s dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left after operating the business and buying necessary equipment and intangible assets. NVIDIA can use it for buybacks, dividends, investments, acquisitions or liquidity. A buyback pays shareholders who sell and reduces the number of shares outstanding; a dividend pays shareholders directly. Because buybacks have become the larger form of return, shareholder payouts have not always matched the cash generated in the same year.

blocks.heading: What could change NVIDIA Corporation’s dividend?

paragraphs.text: NVIDIA has added borrowing to this flexibility. In June 2026 it issued $25 billion of senior unsecured notes for general corporate purposes, including refinancing existing notes. In May it authorized another $80 billion in buybacks and raised its quarterly dividend to $0.25 per share. An authorization is permission, not money already spent; debt is cash today but creates future interest obligations. The test of these choices is therefore not whether NVIDIA can return cash, but whether it can convert the remaining capital into dependable platforms.

Dividends begin at $1.00 per share because the new quarterly rate is $0.25. The base case raises that amount by 5% annually. The bear case holds it flat. The bull case raises it by 25% annually. The modest base path reflects strong cash generation, but also NVIDIA’s preference for buybacks and the board’s continuing discretion over dividends.

earnings.opening: NVIDIA Corporation's next results are expected on November 18, 2026. The key thing to watch is whether it can deliver its platform profitably while managing supply and policy.
earnings.closing: The full memo also explains NVIDIA Corporation’s business, its rivals, its management and its risks.

blocks.heading: What has NVIDIA Corporation guided for the next quarter?

paragraphs.text: Management’s in-force guidance for the quarter to October 2026 is revenue of $105,840 million to $110,160 million. It calls for gross margin of 73.5% to 74.5%. Management’s preliminary outlook calls for roughly 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, while supply limits how much demand it can serve.

The larger promise is preliminary revenue growth of roughly 70% in fiscal 2028. Jensen Huang said NVIDIA had never guided a year ahead before, so this forecast gives investors a new reference point. It is not a guarantee: management says customers want even more, but NVIDIA’s supply chain can support about 70%.

blocks.heading: What were NVIDIA Corporation's last eight quarters of revenue and profit?

paragraphs.text: Gross margin reached 75.0%, while operating income rose to $63,734 million. Net income reached $59,688 million. Yet net income rose only 2% from the preceding quarter even as revenue rose 18%. Large investment gains helped make that comparison less representative of product economics.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in NVIDIA Corporation's next release?

paragraphs.text: NVIDIA has cash and extraordinary demand, but its success now depends on delivery, customer financing, infrastructure and policy. The central question is whether all those pieces arrive together—and produce enough profitable computing work to pay for what comes next.
